newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ minister attacks authors of Australian report.
newsitem.headline: NZ minister attacks authors of Australian report.

text.p: New Zealand's Minister of Maori Affairs has called the authors of a leaked Australian report a "pack of mongrels" and said Canberra should apologise.

Tau Henare's outburst, reported by the New Zealand Herald newspaper, broke a wall of diplomatic silence over Australian attitudes to the country expressed in two leaked secret reports meant to brief Canberra leaders.

His comments were a response to what he called "a nasty attack" on the leader of his New Zealand First Party, Winston Peters, contained in an Australian economic and foreign policy document leaked earlier this month.

The 93-page document was compiled by Australian foreign affairs staff to aid Foreign Minister Alexander Downer and as well as attacking Peters, slated a number of Pacific leaders as corrupt, incompetent or both.
Other New Zealand ministers have played down the significance of this report, which assesses Peters as an ambitious opportunist who enjoys late hours in nightclubs.
Ministers have also kept their counsel over a second paper, made public late on Wednesday, which slams Wellington's defence spending as "inadequate".
In both cases, the government's official line has been that it understands the papers reflect only the views of bureaucrats and not Australian ministers.
Peters, who is Treasurer as well as Deputy Prime Minister, is a central target of both the papers but has said nothing.
He is due to travel to Australia later in the day as one of two cabinet ministers going with Prime Minister Jim Bolger on an extended weekend visit to coincide with a rugby international.
Bolger, Peters and Finance Minister Bill Birch are set to meet their counterparts, including Australian Treasurer Peter Costello, for whose eyes the two secret reports were intended.

The trio have kept their comments on the reports to a minimum, referring obliquely to the clash of the national rugby sides as more important, although Bolger addressed some of the issues raised by the defence report during Thursday.
He told parliament that there was a place for Australia's relationship within a continuing review of defence spending that he expected to be completed later this year.
"Decisions will be considered in the second half of this year, but we have a process in place for working through the questions involved.
"The closer defence relationship (CDR) we have with Australia will be a fundamental factor as Australia is our key ally and security partner," he said.
According to the latest 39-page report, marked 'AUSTEO', or Australian eyes only, even the latest draft of Wellington's defence review would see long-term spending stalled below 1990/91 levels.
The secret document also details a cabinet strategy of Australian ministers pressing the need for bigger military spending on their New Zealand counterparts at every opportunity.

Defence Minister Paul East commented to Radio New Zealand that the cabinet recognised defence spending had been cut substantially since 1988 and there was a need "to at least consider some modest increases".

"The Australian government in its discussions with New Zealand ministers has always made it quite clear that, while it would welcome extra spending, these decisions are matters solely for the New Zealand government.
"At no stage has any undue pressure been brought to bear on any New Zealand minister or on the government," he added.
